explanations: terra: Striving to ruin places where God is remembered supplies another morally failed سَعْي whose object determines its eventual account.
luna: The section’s source gloss says saʿy can be any good or evil work; this verse tells people to race toward good deeds.
terra: A voluntary good act finds God appreciative and knowing, a close nonlexical parallel to striving that is “thanked.”

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss nasīb (نصيب) is a share, and saʿy is work or earning; this verse joins a share to what people earned and says God is swift in reckoning. | terra: They have a نَصِيب from what they earned and God is swift in account, joining the section's audible sense of share to acquisition and reckoning.
terra: The person who turns away strives to corrupt the earth and destroy crops and offspring, giving concrete form to the dictionary claim that سَعْي can be evil work.
luna: The section connects work with satisfaction in God; this verse describes a person who gives up himself seeking God’s approval.
terra: Worldly life deceives rejecters while believers stand above them at Resurrection and God provides without account, linking final rank to unmeasured provision.
terra: The question whether believers calculate they will enter the garden before severe trial challenges an account that expects reward without tested effort.
terra: Those who turn back from faith lose their deeds in both worlds and remain in the Fire, making sustained work end without profitable share.

luna: The section’s dictionary branch for laghw (لغو) includes what is set aside from reckoning; this verse says there is no blame for laghw in oaths, but account is taken for deliberate binding. | terra: God does not take people to account for لَغْو in oaths but does for what hearts earn, exactly joining excluded speech to accountable acquisition.

luna: The section says some effort returns only as fatigue; this verse says showy spending is like dust on a smooth rock, washed away so the giver has nothing left. | terra: A showy charity becomes dust washed from bare rock, leaving its giver unable to gain anything earned; effort and expected wage vanish together.
luna: The section links satisfaction with one’s effort and approval from God; this verse portrays spending for God’s approval as a garden that produces its yield, the fruitful counterpart to 2:264.
terra: A treasured garden burns when its owner is old and dependents are weak, dramatizing the ruin of an expected yield precisely when its wage is needed.
terra: Whatever good people spend is fully repaid to them without wrong, making voluntary expenditure an action with an exact return.

luna: The section says each person’s account belongs to God; this verse warns of the return to Him and full payment for what each soul earned without injustice. | terra: After all are returned to God, each soul is fully paid what it earned, matching the section's sequence of return followed by account.

luna: The section’s saʿy gloss includes work and earning; this verse says each soul has what it earned and bears what it acquired, linking deeds to their own account. | terra: Each soul receives the good it earns and bears the evil it earns, a compact two-sided ledger of acquisition.

luna: The section’s root gh-n-y (غ ن ي) concerns what does not suffice; this verse says wealth and children cannot avail those who disbelieve against God’s judgment, a distinct failure of worldly sufficiency.
terra: Their works fail in this world and the Hereafter and no helpers remain, a repeated formulation of labor stripped of every return.

luna: The section joins work with a final account; this verse describes gathering for a day when each soul is paid in full for what it earned. | terra: When gathered for the certain day, each soul is paid in full for what it earned; gathering makes the wage universal and exact.

luna: The section describes work becoming visible at the account; this verse says each soul will find present what good or evil it did. | terra: Every soul finds the good and evil it did present, matching the face that turns and sees what its labor has become.
terra: Those who believe and do righteous deeds receive their wages in full, directly realizing the dictionary link between intentional work and pay.
luna: The section opens its afterlife account with contrasting faces; this verse also depicts faces turning bright or dark, though it does not connect that appearance to effort.
luna: The section’s two faces carry different outcomes; this verse completes the bright-face side by placing those faces in God’s mercy.
terra: Their spending resembles a freezing wind that destroys a wrongdoer's crop, a concrete agricultural image of expended labor losing its yield.
luna: The section connects effort with a garden and final satisfaction; this verse urges hastening to forgiveness and the Garden prepared for the God-conscious.
terra: Forgiveness and gardens are called an excellent wage for workers, directly pairing عَامِلِين with أَجْر.
terra: The question whether people calculate they will enter the garden before their striving and patience are disclosed links hoped-for reward to proven labor.
terra: On Resurrection Day every soul is fully paid what it earned without wrong, another exact formulation of completed wages.

luna: The section’s satisfied face has a fitting effort; this verse contrasts following God’s approval with earning His anger. | terra: Seeking God's pleasure is set against incurring His wrath, so رضا marks a decisive difference in the final valuation of action.
terra: The two groups have differing degrees with God, giving the opposed relation to divine pleasure in 3:162 a measured outcome.
terra: The faithful rejoice that God does not waste the believers' wage, directly affirming preservation of earned return.

luna: The section asks what effort will earn at the final account; this verse says wages are paid in full on Resurrection and names escape from the Fire and entry into the Garden as success. | terra: Every soul receives its wages in full on Resurrection Day, explicitly locating complete payment after mortal labor.
terra: Guardians must hand over orphan property after assessment and keep no wasteful wage, with God sufficient as حَسِيبًا; stewardship becomes literal reckoning.

luna: The section hears a share in its root gloss for fatigue; this verse explicitly gives men and women a nasīb (نصيب) of what they earned, linking allotted share to labor. | terra: Men and women each have a نَصِيب of what they earn, stating directly that purposeful acquisition produces an apportioned share.

luna: The section’s worker fears effort yielding only fatigue; this verse says God does not wrong even an atom’s weight and multiplies good, assuring exact justice in the return. | terra: God does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies good, joining microscopic accounting to generous payment.

luna: The section’s dictionary form nasīb (نصيب) means a share; this verse says a person who makes a good or bad intercession receives a share of its consequence. | terra: A good intercession yields a نَصِيب from it and an evil one a corresponding burden, extending the share sense to a deliberate intervention's return.
terra: A greeting must be repaid better or equally, and God is حَسِيبًا over everything; measured reciprocation and reckoning occur together.
terra: Whoever does evil is recompensed for it and finds no protector against God, preventing harmful work from escaping settlement.
terra: Believing righteous workers enter the garden without even a speck of wrong, supplying the favorable side of 4:123's deed account.
terra: Believing workers are paid their wages fully and receive additional bounty, showing the wage can exceed the deed without omitting it.
terra: Rejecting faith makes work collapse and leaves the person among afterlife losers, linking null labor to final loss.

luna: The section links laghw (لغو) to speech excluded from an account; this verse distinguishes idle oaths, which are not held to account, from deliberate oaths that carry responsibility. | terra: Laghw in oaths is not taken to account, whereas deliberately bound oaths are; this supplies the section's boundary between surplus and countable intent.

luna: The section’s riḍā gloss names the servant’s pleasure in God and God’s pleasure in the servant; this verse states that mutual approval on the Day when truth benefits. | terra: For the truthful, gardens and mutual satisfaction—رَضِىَ ٱللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا۟ عَنْهُ—form the profitable outcome of the day of accounting.
terra: The Prophet bears none of the believers' account and they bear none of his, guarding the divine ownership of reckoning.
terra: People are returned to God, their true Master, to whom judgment belongs and who is swiftest in account; return and counting meet explicitly.
terra: The God-fearing bear none of the mockers' account but must remind them, joining the section's reminder stance to separated liability.

luna: The section says effort is counted in the final return; this verse assigns people degrees according to what they did and says God is not unaware of their work. | terra: Everyone has ranks according to what they did, so differing labor receives a differentiated outcome under God's complete awareness.
luna: The section’s final reckoning is exact; this verse commands full measure and just weight and forbids burdening a soul beyond its capacity.

luna: The section contrasts worthwhile work with work that yields only fatigue; this verse distinguishes the multiplied return for good from the single measure of evil. | terra: A good deed receives tenfold while an evil deed receives only its like, specifying the just rates in the labor account.
terra: Every soul earns only against itself and no bearer carries another's burden before return to God, defining the account's personal ownership.

luna: The section contrasts outcomes of effort; this verse places the true weighing on that Day and says the heavy scales belong to the successful. | terra: The weighing that day is true, and heavy scales yield success; labor's value is measured rather than merely asserted.

luna: The section’s successful effort yields satisfaction; this verse supplies the reverse side of the scales, where light weight means loss. | terra: Light scales identify those who lost themselves through wrongdoing, the failed side of measured labor.
terra: Garden heirs say they could not have reached it without God's guidance, while the call states they inherited it for their deeds.
terra: Those who deny God's signs have their works nullified and are asked whether they are recompensed except for what they did.
terra: Those who hold to the Book and establish prayer learn that God does not waste the wage of reformers.
terra: Whatever is spent in God's path is fully repaid without injustice, another explicit conversion of purposeful outlay into undiminished wage.
terra: The idolaters' works collapse and they remain in the Fire, a direct pairing of wasted activity with its failed wage.
terra: They enjoyed their allotted share as earlier peoples did, but their works collapsed; temporary portion and final loss meet in one reckoning.

luna: The section makes God’s pleasure part of the good return for effort; this verse calls divine approval greater than the gardens promised to believing men and women. | terra: Gardens and lasting dwellings are promised, but God's pleasure is declared greater, ranking رضا above even the visible wage.

luna: The section describes approval between servant and Lord; this verse applies that mutual pleasure to the foremost believers and promises gardens beneath which rivers flow. | terra: God's pleasure with the faithful and theirs with Him is followed by prepared gardens, again tying reciprocal رضا to final reward.

luna: The section says effort will be seen at the final account; this verse commands people to act and says God, His Messenger, and the believers will see their work. | terra: The command to work is followed by God seeing the work and by return to the Knower, who discloses what was done.

luna: The section’s n-ṣ-b root (ن ص ب) names fatigue, and its hungry worker receives only exhaustion; this verse says fatigue, thirst, and hunger endured in God’s way are recorded as righteous work and their reward is not lost. | terra: Thirst, hunger, and نَصَب in God's path are written as a righteous deed and earn an undiminished wage, reversing toil that yields only toil.

luna: The section says the final account counts deeds; this verse says every small or great expenditure and every valley crossed is recorded so God may reward the best of their work. | terra: Every expenditure and journey is written as a righteous deed so God may reward the best of their work, continuing 9:120's accounting of fatigue itself.
luna: The section’s pleased face belongs to the successful effort; this verse promises those who do good the best reward and describes no gloom covering their faces.
luna: The section contrasts satisfying effort with futile effort; this verse says those who earn evil have faces covered with humiliation.
terra: Those in lasting punishment are asked whether they are being recompensed for anything but what they earned, identifying torment as settled acquisition.
terra: No deed escapes God's witness, not even an atom's weight, and everything is in a clear record; this is exhaustive labor accounting.

luna: The section contrasts a laborer left only with fatigue and one satisfied with their effort; this verse describes full payment for work in worldly life, exposing a reward that may stop there. | terra: Those wanting worldly life receive the full return of their deeds there; 11:16 reveals that this exhausts their wage before the Hereafter.

luna: The section asks whether work has a lasting return; this verse says the deeds of those who seek only worldly life come to nothing in the Hereafter. | terra: For worldly workers only the Fire remains, and what they made is void, the clearest parallel to labor whose sole gain is weariness.
terra: God will pay each group its نَصِيب without diminution, turning the secondary share sense beside نَاصِبَة into exact settlement.
terra: The Lord will fully repay everyone for their deeds and is informed of what they do, joining complete knowledge to full payment.
terra: Patience is commanded because God does not waste the wage of doers of good, setting endurance against fruitless weariness.
terra: Joseph is established in the land and the verse states that God does not waste the wage of doers of good, showing preserved labor in worldly placement.
terra: Joseph says that reverence and patience are not lost because God does not waste the wage of doers of good, explaining his satisfaction after long trial.
terra: The messenger's duty is only delivery while “upon Us is the account,” almost exactly restating the section's division of roles.

luna: The section contrasts effort that bears reward with effort that fails; this verse compares the deeds of disbelievers to ashes scattered by wind, unable to benefit them. | terra: Disbelievers' deeds are ashes scattered by a violent wind and they can gain nothing from what they earned, a vivid image of unusable labor.
terra: God gives from what people ask, yet they cannot enumerate His favors; abundance outruns the creature's حساب while creaturely deeds remain accountable.
terra: God repays each soul for what it earned and is swift in account, making earned outcome the express purpose of the final scene.
terra: No نَصَب touches garden inhabitants and they never leave, opposing both fruitless fatigue and the instability of a merely worldly gain.
terra: Humans cannot enumerate God's favors, reversing the direction of the section's final count: divine gifts exceed human counting while God counts people.

luna: The section contrasts temporary exhaustion with a lasting return for worthy effort; this verse says what people have runs out while what is with God remains, and the patient receive their wage. | terra: What humans possess runs out while what is with God remains, and patient people are paid by their best deeds; enduring wage answers expended labor.

luna: The section’s worker expects a return for effort; this verse promises a good life and full wage for whoever does good work, male or female. | terra: Righteous work receives a good life and a reward based on the best deeds, directly linking labor, pleasing life, and payment.

luna: The section ties work to a final reckoning; this verse says every soul is paid in full for what it did and is not wronged. | terra: On the day each soul pleads for itself, it is fully paid for what it did without wrong, an individualized work account.
terra: Doing good benefits the doer and doing evil harms the doer, expressing the return of labor upon its worker.

luna: The section describes a final account belonging to God; this verse says each person’s record will be brought out on the Day of Resurrection. | terra: Each person's record is fastened to them and brought out as an open book, concretely attaching the account to its worker.

luna: The section says ḥisāb (حساب) is counting things; here the person is told to read their book and is sufficient as their own reckoner. | terra: The person is told to read their own record and is sufficient that day as an accountant against themself, joining self-inspection, sufficiency, and reckoning.
terra: One who wants the immediate life receives only the allotted portion God wills and then Hell, the deliberately failed counterpart to the afterlife striving in 17:19.

luna: The section calls saʿy work and earning; here those who seek the Hereafter and strive for it have saʿy that is acknowledged, the fulfilled counterpart to labor left only as fatigue. | terra: One who wants the Hereafter and makes its due striving has effort that is thanked, directly naming successful labor and its reception.
terra: God extends His gift to both the immediate-life seeker and the afterlife striver, clarifying that present provision alone is not the final labor verdict.
terra: Worldly preferences differ, but the Hereafter has greater ranks and preference; this explains the larger return of the striving in 17:19.
luna: The section’s account counts things and the worker expects a due return; this verse commands full measure and a straight balance, making fairness in allotment concrete.

luna: The section weighs whether effort yields a wage; this verse says God does not let the wage of one who does good work go to waste, the direct assurance opposite the futile labor. | terra: God says He does not waste the wage of anyone who does good work, the positive boundary against labor yielding only fatigue.

luna: The section ends with God’s account; this verse opens the book and says it leaves out neither small nor large deeds, which are found present without injustice. | terra: The record leaves neither small nor great without counting it and people find their deeds present, concretely staging the section's enumeration.

luna: The section’s n-ṣ-b root (ن ص ب) names fatigue; Moses’ companion uses that same root for weariness from their journey, a concrete bodily-fatigue scene though this verse does not weigh its reward. | terra: Moses' companion says their journey has brought نَصَب, a concrete instance of purposeful movement leaving fatigue on the traveler.
terra: The question about the greatest losers in deeds introduces the people whose miscalculated striving is specified in 18:104.

luna: The section names saʿy and describes work that yields only exhaustion; this verse says some people’s saʿy has gone astray while they think they did good work, with the root ḥ-s-b in their mistaken reckoning. | terra: Their striving is lost in worldly life while they calculate that they work well; this joins wasted effort to a mistaken reckoning.
terra: Their works collapse and receive no weight on Resurrection Day, completing the lost striving and wrong calculation of 18:104.
terra: Hell is named as the recompense of those whose striving was lost and whose deeds had no weight in 18:104-105.
terra: Believing workers receive gardens as hospitality, supplying the deliberate opposite outcome to the lost workers of 18:103-105.

luna: The section joins work to the final account; this verse says whoever hopes to meet the Lord should do righteous work, directly linking effort with that meeting. | terra: Whoever hopes to meet the Lord must do righteous work sincerely, joining purposeful action to the encounter where the account occurs.

luna: The section says no laghiya is heard in the garden; this verse likewise says its people will hear no idle speech there, only a greeting of peace. | terra: Garden inhabitants hear no لَغْو, only peace, while their provision arrives continually; absence of emptiness accompanies sufficient provision.
terra: God says He is counting for the rejecters a count, a non-ḥisāb formulation of the deliberate divine enumeration developed in the section.
terra: God has encompassed people and counted them exactly, a direct formulation of the section's counting sense of account.
terra: Each person comes to God individually, showing the personal presentation produced by the exact count in 19:94.
terra: The Hour is coming so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for, an exact statement of effort entering God's account.
terra: Adam is warned that expulsion from the garden would make him toil, locating weariness outside the garden where the satisfied face rests.
terra: Inside the garden Adam neither hungers nor lacks clothing, the direct positive boundary to food that does not avail against hunger.
terra: The garden also removes thirst and exposure to heat, completing the sufficient provision opposed to punishment's useless food and drink.

luna: The section ends with God’s account; this verse sets just scales on the Day of Resurrection and says even a mustard seed is not lost, showing how exact the reckoning is. | terra: Just scales omit nothing even as small as a mustard seed, and كَفَىٰ بِنَا حَاسِبِينَ joins exact reckoning to divine sufficiency.
luna: The section joins effort with its reckoning; here no effort of a believer is denied and it is written down, so the reader sees both recognition and record.
terra: Those who strive to frustrate God's signs are assigned the Blaze, explicitly giving hostile striving its corresponding wage.

luna: The section’s word laghiya names empty speech; this verse portrays believers turning away from laghw, the worldly counterpart to a garden where it is not heard. | terra: Believers turn away from لَغْو in worldly life; their deliberate refusal anticipates the garden where such speech is not heard at all.
terra: A record speaks truth and no one is wronged, while obligation stays within capacity; the account measures real work without manufacturing impossible liability.

luna: The section distinguishes effort by its final outcome; here heavy scales mark those who succeed at the reckoning. | terra: Those whose scales are heavy prosper, a direct parallel to effort whose final weight satisfies its owner.

luna: The section sets satisfaction against wasted effort; here light scales leave their bearers lost, the adverse outcome to the heavy measure in 23:102. | terra: Those whose scales are light lose themselves and remain in Hell, making deficient labor produce the opposite wage.
terra: Fire scorches their faces after the light-scale verdict in 23:103, returning the failed reckoning visibly to the face.
terra: God asks whether people calculated that they were created pointlessly and would not return, directly opposing the denial of return and account.

luna: The section’s hungry laborer gets no satisfying return; this verse pictures a thirsty person pursuing a mirage and finding nothing, then meeting God’s full account. | terra: Works become a thirsting person's mirage; the false estimate يَحْسَبُهُ ends when God fully settles حِسَابَهُ, uniting insufficiency, miscount, and payment.

luna: The section contrasts effort that is rewarded with effort that leaves only fatigue; here deeds are made scattered dust, a concrete image of work with no lasting return. | terra: Deeds are confronted and made scattered dust, a concrete realization of work whose worker receives no gain from it.

luna: The section connects laghw with empty speech; this verse says the servants of the Merciful pass by such speech with dignity, a conduct parallel to its absence in the garden. | terra: God's servants pass by لَغْو with dignity, a lived counterpart to the final environment from which vain speech has disappeared.
terra: On the final day wealth and children do not avail, setting a sharp limit on what can count as sufficient capital.
terra: Only one who comes with a sound heart escapes the insufficiency named in 26:88, identifying what remains valid at the account.
terra: Noah says his followers' account rests only with his Lord, the same boundary that reserves final counting to God.
terra: Faces are cast into the fire and asked whether they are repaid except for what they did, visibly joining deed, wage, and punished face.

luna: The section’s word laghiya is idle speech; this verse describes believers turning away when they hear laghw, a concrete response to the same kind of talk. | terra: When believers hear لَغْو they turn away and distinguish “our deeds” from “your deeds,” tightly linking discarded speech with separate labor accounts.
luna: The section’s nasīb (نصيب) is an allotted share; this verse speaks of one’s share in worldly life, distinguishing that limited portion from the enduring return discussed in the section.

luna: The section’s successful worker is satisfied in a garden; this verse promises lofty chambers in the Garden to those who believe and do good work. | terra: Believing workers are lodged in high garden chambers, followed by “excellent is the wage of workers,” a close labor-to-height correspondence.
luna: The section links a good return to effort; this neighboring verse identifies patient endurance and trust in the Lord as the qualities of those receiving the promised chambers.
luna: The section describes saʿy as effort; this verse says those who strive for God are guided by Him and are with the good-doers.

luna: The section treats even empty excess as omitted from a count; this verse says God can bring a deed to light even if it is a mustard seed hidden in a rock or in the heavens or earth. | terra: Even a mustard-seed weight hidden in rock, heaven, or earth is brought by God, showing that no minute work can escape the account.

luna: The section links effort to a return; this verse says no soul knows the hidden comfort prepared as a reward for what people did. | terra: No soul knows the comfort hidden for them as recompense for what they did, showing a wage whose sufficiency surpasses the worker's present sight.
terra: There is no blame for an honest mistake, only for what hearts intend, defining the purposeful boundary that makes an act accountable work.
terra: Not an atom's weight or anything smaller or greater escapes God; all is in a clear record, specifying the precision of final counting.
terra: Those who strive against God's signs receive painful punishment, a repeated negative instance of effort measured by its aim.
terra: Striving to defeat God's signs ends with the strivers brought into punishment, making failed hostile effort visible at its destination.
luna: The section contrasts empty speech with accounted effort; this verse says good words rise to God and righteous work lifts them, connecting speech to valued action.
terra: Reciters, prayer, and giving form a trade that does not fail because God pays their wages fully and adds bounty.
terra: Garden inhabitants say no نَصَب or weariness touches them there, the exact reversal of a face whose labor remains upon it as exhaustion.
terra: God writes what people sent ahead and their traces and enumerates everything in a clear register, a direct image of comprehensive counting.

luna: The section says the account is for the people’s deeds; this verse states that each person is repaid only for what they used to do. | terra: On that day no soul is wronged and people are recompensed only for what they did, stating the exact labor settlement.
terra: The condemned are recompensed only for what they used to do, defining punishment as the corresponding wage of action.
terra: After the garden victory, “for the like of this let the workers work” makes that result the proper object of purposeful labor.
luna: The section contrasts garden reward with failed food; this verse asks whether the sinners’ welcome is the tree of Zaqqūm, a punishment meal.
luna: The section’s failed food belongs to punishment; this neighboring verse locates the Zaqqūm tree at the root of Hell.
luna: The section’s food scene is a sign of the failed outcome; this verse describes the frightening fruit of the punishment tree.
luna: The section’s food does not nourish or satisfy hunger; this verse says the condemned eat from the tree and fill their bellies, a meal that fills without restoring them.
luna: The section contrasts nourishment with hunger; this neighboring verse says the tree’s food is followed by a mixture of boiling water.
terra: God asks whether righteous workers could be treated like corrupters, defining fair reckoning through the required distinction between their labors.
terra: Solomon is told that God's gift may be bestowed or withheld without account, placing sovereign abundance beyond the finite counting applied to human work.
terra: Job names his affliction as نُصْب and torment, confirming the fatigue sense heard in the worked and weary face without itself supplying a wage scene.
terra: God is pleased with gratitude while every soul bears only its own burden, linking divine رضا to individualized responsibility.

luna: The section defines ḥ-s-b as counting things; this verse promises the patient their wage without account, using account to mark a reward beyond measure. | terra: The patient are paid their wage without measure, a concrete boundary to “account” as finite enumeration.
terra: What earlier rejecters earned did not avail them, making acquisition itself incapable of becoming sufficient protection.
terra: The evils they earned then struck them, supplying the actual wage after 39:50 denies that their gains could avail.

luna: The section’s work and its return meet in the final account; this verse says every soul is paid in full for what it did. | terra: Every soul is paid in full for what it did, and God best knows their deeds; complete knowledge grounds complete settlement.
terra: Garden inheritors praise the fulfilled promise and the verse concludes “excellent is the wage of workers,” naming the garden as earned pay.

luna: The section ends by assigning the account to God; this verse says each soul is recompensed for what it earned and declares there is no injustice that Day. | terra: Every soul is recompensed for what it earned with no injustice and a swift account, directly combining acquisition, wage, and reckoning.
terra: Righteous workers enter the garden and are provided for بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ, contrasting exact deed reckoning with reward beyond measure.
terra: Past peoples' abundant acquisitions did not avail them, another direct use of earning followed by failed sufficiency.
luna: The section ends with God’s account; this verse says hearing, sight, and skin testify against people about what they did.
luna: The section’s account makes deeds answerable; this neighboring verse explains how the skins testify, saying God enabled them to speak.
terra: Rejecters command one another to make noise, وَٱلْغَوْا, during the Quran; their manufactured babble contrasts with the garden where no vain speech is heard.

luna: The section distinguishes effort by its result; this verse says good work benefits its doer and evil work returns against its doer, while God wrongs no servant. | terra: Righteous work benefits its doer and evil works against its doer, while the Lord wrongs no servant; action returns to its source justly.

luna: The section’s nasīb (نصيب) gloss is an allotted share; this verse contrasts a share of the Hereafter’s harvest with having no share there for the one who seeks only this world. | terra: The seeker of the worldly harvest receives some of it but has no afterlife share, while the afterlife harvest is increased; aim determines labor's return.
terra: Whoever earns a good deed receives increase in it and God is appreciative, explaining how a worker's gain can be acknowledged beyond bare equivalence.

luna: The section’s satisfied effort ends in a garden; this verse tells its people they inherit the Garden for what they used to do. | terra: The garden is inherited because of what its people used to do, identifying the lasting habitation as labor's return.
luna: The section’s food scene separates punishment from reward; this verse names Zaqqūm as the sinners’ food.
luna: The section’s meal does not satisfy; this neighboring verse identifies Zaqqūm as the food of the sinner.
luna: The section’s failed food is a punishment scene; this verse describes the tree’s contents boiling in the belly.
luna: The section contrasts sustenance with torment; this verse completes the punishment-food image by comparing it to boiling water.
terra: Neither what they earned nor their protectors avail them before Hell, uniting useless gain, failed sufficiency, and punishment.
terra: Whoever works righteousness does so for themself and whoever does evil works against themself, before all return to the Lord.
terra: Evildoers wrongly calculate that they will be made equal to believing righteous workers; the verse rejects an undifferentiated wage.

luna: The section joins labor with recompense; this verse says every soul is repaid for what it earned without being wronged. | terra: Each soul is recompensed for what it earned without wrong, a compact formulation of labor, settlement, and exact justice.
terra: God's record speaks truth because what people did was copied, giving the labor account a concrete written form.

luna: The section asks what each effort receives; this verse assigns people degrees according to their work and promises their deeds will be paid in full. | terra: People have ranks according to their deeds so that God may pay their works in full, turning qualitative labor into an undiminished allocation.

luna: The section depicts effort that can go astray and fail to return; this verse says the deeds of those who disbelieve and turn others from God’s way are made to stray. | terra: Those who disbelieve and block God's way have their deeds led astray, describing purposeful activity deprived of its intended return.
terra: Believers who do righteous work have their evils removed and their state repaired, the paired successful side of the failed deeds in 47:1.
terra: Because they hated what God sent down, He made their works collapse; rejection removes the hoped-for return of labor.
terra: Following what angers God and disliking His pleasure causes works to collapse, tying divine رضا and the survival of deeds together.
terra: God is pleased with the believers' pledged intention and rewards them with a near victory, a historical instance of divine رضا becoming recompense.
terra: The faithful seek bounty and divine pleasure, and righteous workers among them are promised forgiveness and a great wage.

luna: The section says empty speech is absent from the garden and that account belongs to God; this verse introduces two receivers seated on either side before the next verse says every utterance is watched.

luna: The section hears laghw (لغو) as empty or excess speech and as what is dropped from an account; this verse says every utterance has a watcher ready, making the contrast with garden speech concrete. | terra: No utterance escapes an observing recorder; alongside the oath exceptions in 2:225 and 5:89, this distinguishes recording speech from liability for laghw.
terra: Garden residents are told to eat and drink pleasantly for what they used to do, making satisfying food the direct pay of action.

luna: The section contrasts reward with fruitless labor; this verse promises that believers’ deeds will not be diminished and that each person is held to what they earned. | terra: Each person is a pledge for what they earned even when believing families are reunited, preserving the individual labor account.
luna: The section contrasts food that cannot sustain with a garden reward; this verse promises the garden people fruit and meat of what they desire.

luna: The section’s garden has no laghw; this verse says there is neither idle speech nor sin in the garden scene. | terra: The garden cup contains neither لَغْو nor sin, placing the same excluded speech amid the rewarded hospitality described by the section.

luna: The section treats effort as the basis of recompense; this verse says those who did evil and those who did good are repaid for what they did. | terra: God repays those who do evil for what they did and those who do good with the best, stating the two wages of action.
terra: The verse points to what is in Moses' scrolls, locating the labor-account rule of 53:39 in the source tradition named by the section.
terra: Abraham who fulfilled is named beside Moses, completing the scriptural attribution that frames the rules in 53:38-41.
terra: No bearer bears another's burden; just before the rule about striving, this makes each labor account personally nontransferable.

luna: The section’s source root saʿy (س ع ي) names effort for earnings; this verse says a person has only what they strove for, making effort the basis of the allotment. | terra: The rule that a person has only what they strive for makes سَعَى the precise basis of the section's labor account.

luna: The section says the satisfied face looks back at its saʿy; this verse says that effort will be seen, so the work itself comes into view at judgment. | terra: The person's striving will be seen, matching the satisfied face that turns back and sees what its effort produced.

luna: The section contrasts exhausting work with work that brings satisfaction; this verse completes the sequence by promising full recompense for effort. | terra: Full recompense completes the section's sequence from intentional work through inspection to an undiminished wage.
terra: The final destination is to the Lord, completing the effort-and-recompense sequence of 53:39-41 with the owner of the account.
terra: God alone enriches and grants sufficiency, setting the source of genuine غِنَى against food, wealth, and earnings that fail to avail.
terra: Everything people did is in the records, locating intentional acts inside the final inventory.
terra: Every small and great matter is inscribed, specifying the exhaustive scale of the deed records named in 54:52.
luna: The section ends with God’s account; this verse says God set up the balance, giving a concrete image of measured judgment.
luna: The section describes deeds being counted; this verse commands that the balance not be transgressed, adding the demand for a just measure.
luna: The section contrasts effort that yields satisfaction with effort that fails; this verse requires weighing with justice and forbids giving short measure.
luna: The section’s satisfied worker receives a fitting return; this verse states the principle that the reward of good is good.
luna: The section’s food leaves hunger; this verse gives garden people fruit they choose, the provision opposite an unsatisfying meal.
luna: The section’s hungry face has no satisfying food; this verse adds desired bird meat to the garden’s provision.
terra: Garden provision is recompense for what its people used to do; 56:25 then specifies that vain speech is absent from that earned setting.

luna: The section describes a garden without laghiya; this verse says its people hear neither idle nor sinful speech there. | terra: Garden residents hear neither لَغْوًا nor sinful speech, a direct lexical and scenic parallel to the section's silent garden.
terra: Peace is the only speech heard, positively completing the absence of vain speech stated in 56:25.
luna: The section’s hungry face receives unusable food; this verse gives the condemned Zaqqūm as their food.
luna: The section says its food does not satisfy hunger; this verse says the condemned fill their bellies with the punishment tree, which only loads the body before further torment.
luna: The section contrasts nourishment with an unsatisfying meal; this neighboring verse follows the tree with boiling water to drink.
luna: The section’s hunger is not relieved by its food; this verse completes the punishment-drink scene by comparing the drinking to thirsty camels.
luna: The section’s saʿy is effort directed toward a result; this verse tells people to race toward forgiveness and a garden, making striving for the lasting reward explicit.
terra: Monasticism is invented seeking God's pleasure but not duly observed; believers among them receive wages, bringing intention, failed performance, رضا, and pay together.
terra: God has enumerated deeds that their doers forgot, sharply distinguishing divine counting from the worker's incomplete memory.

luna: The section joins the pleased servant with divine approval; this verse states both sides of that approval and pairs it with abiding gardens. | terra: God is pleased with a faithful people and they with Him, then admits them to gardens; divine approval and human contentment meet in the wage.
terra: Whoever relies on God finds that He is حَسْبُهُ, using the account root's sufficiency branch to locate enoughness in the giver rather than the wage.
terra: Disbelievers are told not to excuse themselves that day because they are repaid only for what they did, making the account answer deed rather than plea.

luna: The section weighs effort by what it yields; this verse says life and death were made to test who is best in deed. | terra: Life and death are created to test who is best in deed, making purposeful work the object of divine assessment.
terra: God asks whether those who submit could be made like criminals, rejecting a reckoning that gives opposed workers the same wage.
terra: “What is wrong with you; how do you judge?” exposes the faulty calculation behind the impossible equality posed in 68:35.
terra: On the day of presentation nothing about the people remains hidden, establishing the disclosure in which effort and its record are faced.

luna: The section cites the joy of the person given the book from the right; this verse supplies that book-giving scene and starts the contrast of outcomes. | terra: Receiving the record in the right hand identifies the speaker whose confidence about his account follows in 69:20.

luna: The section explicitly cites this speaker expecting to meet his ḥisāb (حساب); his confidence makes the account itself something anticipated rather than feared. | terra: The right-book recipient says he expected to meet his account, the closest parallel to a face looking back contentedly on its labor.

luna: The section cites this person’s satisfied life after the account; it gives a concrete image of the return from the book and reckoning. | terra: The resulting عِيشَةٍ رَاضِيَةٍ repeats the section's satisfaction vocabulary and locates it after a favorable account.

luna: The section connects satisfied effort with a high garden; this verse places the person in a high garden after receiving the book. | terra: A high garden is the place of the pleasing life in 69:21, matching the high garden reached by the satisfied face.
luna: The section’s satisfied face is in a garden; this neighboring verse makes its fruit near and accessible, a concrete sign of the reward.

luna: The section says saʿy is labor or earning; this verse tells the garden people to eat and drink for what they sent ahead in earlier days. | terra: Eating and drinking are explicitly granted for what was sent ahead in former days, turning sufficient garden provision into the wage of work.

luna: The section sets the pleased account against futile effort; this verse begins the reversed book scene with the person receiving the record in the left hand. | terra: Receiving the record in the left hand stages the opposite worker before his rejection of the account in 69:26.

luna: The section explicitly cites the left-handed speaker who wishes not to know his ḥisāb (حساب), the adverse counterpart to the joyful meeting in 69:20. | terra: The left-book recipient wishes he had never known his account, reversing the confident meeting of the account in 69:20.

luna: The section’s root gh-n-y (غ ن ي) concerns what is sufficient; after the failed account, this speaker says his wealth did not avail him, a distinct but pointed failure of sufficiency. | terra: The condemned speaker says his wealth did not avail him, using أَغْنَى in the section's sense of failing to suffice at reckoning.

luna: The section contrasts those whose effort earns a garden with those left hungry; this verse names the adverse person’s failure to urge feeding the poor, a concrete neglected deed before the punishment meal.
luna: The section describes food that does not satisfy hunger; this verse gives another punishment meal, with no food except ghislin.
luna: The section’s inadequate food belongs to a failed outcome; this neighboring verse says only sinners eat the punishment food in 69:36.
luna: The section’s share gloss is an allotted portion; this verse describes a known right in the wealth of the righteous, a portion set aside for others.
luna: The section develops the idea of an allotted share; this neighboring verse names the asker and deprived as recipients of the known right in 70:24.
terra: God encompasses what His messengers carry and counts everything numerically, extending divine counting to exhaustive knowledge.
luna: The section describes food that cannot relieve hunger; this verse gives the punished person choking food, another scene where eating is torment rather than provision.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss for saʿy includes earning; this verse says each soul is held for what it earned. | terra: Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned, making acquisition an inescapably personal liability.

luna: The section makes effort and its return visible at the account; this verse says a person will be told what they sent ahead and left behind. | terra: The human is informed of what was sent ahead and left behind, making the final account include the full temporal reach of action.
luna: The section says one face looks at its effort and is satisfied; this verse makes the person a witness against their own deeds.
luna: The section’s account exposes what effort produced; this neighboring verse completes the self-witness scene by saying excuses will not conceal it.
luna: The section makes the face that sees its effort and is satisfied visible; this verse portrays radiant faces on the Day of Resurrection, a parallel outward sign of a favorable outcome.
luna: The section’s satisfied face turns toward its result; this verse depicts the radiant faces looking toward their Lord, without explicitly naming their deeds.
luna: The section contrasts two kinds of face and the return of their efforts; this verse gives the opposite portrait of faces that day, gloomy.
luna: The section’s adverse face ends in a failed outcome; this neighboring verse says those gloomy faces expect a backbreaking calamity.
terra: The human wrongly calculates that he will be left aimless, a mistaken حساب-like assumption that would erase purposeful work and final settlement.
terra: Feeding the needy, orphan, and captive is the concrete deed whose disavowal of human payment follows in 76:9 and whose divine wage appears in 76:12 and 76:22.

luna: The section treats effort as seeking a return; this verse depicts people feeding others for God’s sake without wanting recompense or thanks from them. | terra: The righteous feed others while seeking neither human recompense nor thanks, qualifying the section's wage principle: their intended pay is from God.
terra: God recompenses their patience with a garden and silk, explicitly making the garden hospitality that culminates in 76:22 a wage.
terra: Silver vessels and cups circulate among the garden people, supplying the particular hospitality immediately before their striving is pronounced thanked in 76:22.
terra: The silver vessels are precisely measured, adding measured provision to the garden scene whose guests' effort receives acknowledgment in 76:22.

luna: The section contrasts a drink that cannot help hunger with a good return; this verse gives the righteous a pure drink from their Lord. | terra: The Lord clothes the garden people and gives them a pure drink; this is the last concrete gift before 76:22 identifies the whole reception as their wage.

luna: The section’s pleased face is satisfied with its effort; in this garden scene the people are told their saʿy was appreciated, making the reward visible after hospitality. | terra: Garden residents are told that their striving was thanked, the direct counterpart of the face pleased with its own effort.
terra: The righteous eat and drink pleasantly for what they used to do, reversing food that cannot satisfy hunger.
terra: God says this is how doers of good are recompensed, explicitly interpreting the sufficient provision of 77:43 as their wage.
luna: The section contrasts efforts by whether they stand at the account; this verse identifies people who did not expect any reckoning, a stance that precedes their failed outcome.

luna: The section defines account as counting things; this verse says everything has been counted and recorded in a book. | terra: God says every thing has been enumerated in a record, a literal counterpart to the section's definition of account as counting things one by one.

luna: The section’s dictionary form laghw names empty speech and the garden is free of it; this verse says there is no idle talk or falsehood there. | terra: No vain speech or lie is heard in the garden, directly paralleling the garden from which لَاغِيَة is absent.

luna: The section names ḥ-s-b as counting and also cites its dictionary sense of sufficiency; this verse calls the recompense an adequate gift from the Lord. | terra: The righteous receive recompense as عَطَاءً حِسَابًا, the sufficient gift that answers labor whose provision did not suffice.
terra: The great overwhelming event arrives, naming the event at which 79:35 says each person remembers their striving.

luna: The section links saʿy to the final reckoning; this verse says people will remember what they strove for on the day of the great event. | terra: At the overwhelming event the human remembers what they strove for, staging the retrospective inspection of labor described in the section.
terra: Hell is exposed to everyone who can see immediately after remembered striving, turning the review of work into a visible outcome.
terra: The transgressor opens the failed branch of the reckoning that follows the recollection of striving in 79:35.
terra: Preferring the nearer life identifies the aim of the failed worker whose destination 79:39 states.
terra: Hell is the abode of the one who preferred worldly life, completing the negative wage of 79:37-38.
terra: Fearing the Lord's station and restraining desire identify the contrary labor whose destination follows in 79:41.
terra: The garden is the abode of the self-restraining person, completing the successful wage after striving is remembered.
luna: The section follows a face’s effort to its final state; this verse shows radiant faces on that Day.
luna: The section’s satisfied face is an outward sign of its return; this verse describes some faces as laughing and rejoicing.
luna: The section divides faces by outcome; this verse begins the opposed portrait of dust-covered faces.
luna: The section contrasts a satisfied result with a failed one; this verse says other faces are covered with darkness.
luna: The section’s two faces mark divergent outcomes; this neighboring verse identifies the dust-covered, dark faces as those of disbelievers.
luna: The section ends with the account of people’s deeds; this verse introduces guardians appointed over them, setting up the recorders named next.

luna: The section’s account counts what people did; this neighboring verse identifies the appointed guardians as noble recorders. | terra: Honored guardians are recording scribes; 82:12 identifies deeds as the material they know.

luna: The section’s ḥisāb (حساب) is counting things; this verse says the recorders know what people do, the specific content of that account. | terra: The recorders know whatever people do, directly supplying the inventory behind the final reckoning.
luna: The section asks what effort earns and describes a share of work; this verse condemns those who shortchange others, introducing a reversal of fair return.
luna: The section treats effort and its due share; this verse says the defrauders demand full measure when they take from people.
luna: The section’s laborer expects a return; this verse says the defrauders give others less when measuring or weighing for them, the unjust opposite of a fair recompense.
luna: The section’s pleased face looks back at its effort; this verse makes the faces of the rewarded people recognizable by the radiance of bliss.
luna: The section contrasts food that cannot satisfy hunger with the garden reward; this verse gives the righteous a sealed drink of pure nectar.
luna: The section names saʿy as earning work; this verse says the seal is musk and calls competitors to compete for that reward.
luna: The section’s garden reward answers failed sustenance; this neighboring verse says the pure drink is mixed with Tasnīm.
luna: The section contrasts an unsatisfying meal with garden provision; this verse completes the drink scene by identifying Tasnīm as a spring from which those brought near drink.
terra: The closing question asks whether disbelievers have been repaid for what they used to do, presenting final recompense as the verdict on their conduct.

luna: The section follows the worker’s effort to its reckoning; this verse portrays each person laboring toward the Lord and meeting Him, compressing effort and encounter into one scene. | terra: The human toils toward the Lord and will meet Him, concentrating purposeful weariness, return, and the encounter at which labor is assessed.

luna: The section contrasts two faces by their effort and outcome; this verse opens the parallel scene of receiving one’s book in the right hand. | terra: Receiving the book in the right hand identifies the favorable account holder before 84:8 states that his reckoning is easy.

luna: The section ends with ḥisāb (حساب); this verse says the person will have an easy account, the favorable side of that reckoning. | terra: The right-book recipient receives an easy account, a close enactment of the reckoning that belongs to God alone.

luna: The section’s face is pleased with its effort; this verse shows the right-handed person returning to their family rejoicing. | terra: After the easy account the recipient returns joyfully, clarifying how satisfaction follows a favorable labor account.

luna: The section’s positive account has an opposite; this verse gives the other person’s book from behind their back. | terra: Receiving the book behind the back identifies the failed account holder before his call for destruction in 84:11.

luna: The section contrasts satisfying and failed effort; this neighboring verse gives the despairing response to the adverse book, a wish for destruction. | terra: The other recipient calls for destruction after receiving the record behind his back; 84:10 identifies the failed side of the same account scene.

luna: The section contrasts the fates that follow effort; this verse completes the adverse book scene with entry into the blaze. | terra: His entry into a blaze supplies the wage of the failed account begun in 84:10-11, like labor ending only in punishment.

luna: The section’s faces are divided by what their effort yields; this verse says the person in the adverse book had lived happily among their family before the return. | terra: His former joy among his family contrasts with the lasting joy after an easy account and explains the false expectation of no return in 84:14.

luna: The section ends with a reckoning; this verse explains the contrast by the adverse person’s belief that they would not return. | terra: He had calculated that he would never return, exposing the false reckoning corrected by the section's assertion that return and account are God's.

luna: The section says God owns the final account; this verse completes the book scene by saying the person’s Lord was watching them. | terra: The Lord had always seen him; this explains why the mistaken confidence in 84:14 cannot remove any work from the final account.
luna: The section links effort and its final satisfaction; this verse calls to the tranquil soul as it returns to its Lord.

luna: The section defines riḍā (رضا) as approval between servant and Lord; this verse describes the soul as pleased and pleasing as it returns. | terra: The soul returns رَاضِيَةً مَرْضِيَّةً, expressing in one line both the servant's satisfaction and God's satisfaction named in the section.
luna: The section’s satisfied soul is given a garden; this neighboring verse welcomes that soul among God’s servants.

luna: The section links approval with garden reward; this neighboring verse completes the welcome by commanding the soul to enter the Garden. | terra: The mutually satisfied soul of 89:28 enters God's garden, completing the same movement from accepted labor to a satisfying garden.
terra: Humanity is created in toil, broadening the worked face's exhaustion into the ordinary condition from which the final wage acquires urgency.

luna: The section divides faces by the result of their effort; this verse states that human saʿy is diverse, framing different labor and outcomes. | terra: “Your striving is diverse” makes labor the fork from which the surah's opposed outcomes of ease and hardship proceed.

luna: The section’s satisfied face has effort that yielded well; this verse begins the opposite path from futile labor, describing giving and God-consciousness. | terra: Giving and guarding oneself begin the successful form of the diverse striving announced in 92:4.

luna: The section weighs effort by what it yields; this verse describes affirming the good promise, the belief that accompanies the path of giving. | terra: Affirming the best promise supplies the conviction that directs the giver's effort toward its favorable result.

luna: The section contrasts effort ending in strain with effort ending in satisfaction; this verse promises that the giver’s path will be made easy. | terra: God eases the giver toward ease, making rightly aimed striving issue in a fitting path and outcome.

luna: The section’s root gh-n-y (غ ن ي) appears in the idea of what does not suffice; here wealth will not avail its owner at the fall, a distinct but pointed form of insufficiency. | terra: Withholding and deeming oneself self-sufficient, ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ, begin the failed branch of striving and expose false sufficiency as its motive.

luna: The section’s face is pleased with its effort; this verse sets against it the one who denies the good promise. | terra: Denying the best promise supplies the orientation that makes the miser's effort fail.

luna: The section portrays effort that leaves a person exhausted; this verse says the path of the denier will be eased toward hardship. | terra: God eases the miser toward hardship, giving the second form of diverse striving its contrary result.
terra: The miser's wealth will not avail him when he falls, using يُغْنِى in the same failed-sufficiency sense as the useless food.
terra: God says guidance rests upon Him in the same passage that separates diverse strivings and their outcomes.
terra: The first life and the Hereafter belong to God, grounding His authority over both the labor period and its final wage.
luna: The section treats saʿy as work with a return; this verse depicts giving wealth to purify oneself, an action whose aim is not immediate gain.

luna: The section asks what a person’s effort earns; this verse says the giver seeks no repayment from anyone for a favor owed, clarifying the intended direction of the deed. | terra: The giver acts without any person's favor needing repayment, excluding social exchange from the labor account that ends in satisfaction.

luna: The section describes satisfaction with one’s effort and mutual approval; this verse makes seeking the face of the Most High the aim of giving. | terra: The giver seeks only the face of the Most High, fixing the aim that makes the satisfaction promised in 92:21 a divine wage.

luna: The section’s pleased face sees a worthy result from its effort; this verse ends the giving passage with the giver becoming satisfied. | terra: After giving for God's approval, the person “will surely be satisfied,” making رضا the end of a correctly directed striving.
terra: The Lord will give until the addressee is satisfied, pairing divine gift with رضا even though the verse does not itself name the preceding work.
terra: The command فَٱنصَبْ after finishing directs renewed exertion toward the Lord, setting purposeful fatigue on the successful side of labor.
terra: Human transgression begins when a person treats himself as independent, introducing the false sufficiency named in 96:7.
terra: Seeing oneself as ٱسْتَغْنَى is the opposite of recognizing that created gains cannot suffice at the final account.
terra: The return is to the Lord despite the person's claim of self-sufficiency, correcting that claim through the same return-account sequence as the section.

luna: The section defines mutual riḍā (رضا); this verse says God is pleased with the believers and they are pleased with Him, as their reward is gardens. | terra: Everlasting gardens are the reward where God is pleased with them and they with Him, explicitly realizing both directions of رضا.

luna: The section says effort will be accounted for; this verse depicts people coming out in separate groups to be shown their deeds. | terra: People emerge separately to be shown their deeds, establishing the display whose smallest entries 99:7-8 then specify.

luna: The section’s account takes each deed into view; this verse says even an atom’s weight of good will be seen. | terra: An atom's weight of good is seen, matching the section's claim that labor itself will be looked upon and counted.

luna: The section contrasts efforts that satisfy and efforts that fail; this verse makes even an atom’s weight of evil visible too. | terra: An atom's weight of evil is likewise seen, preventing failed effort from disappearing outside the account.

luna: The section’s account counts and evaluates; this verse makes the weighing of deeds the scene that determines each person’s outcome. | terra: Heavy scales identify the favorable measurement whose result is the pleasing life in 101:7.

luna: The section explicitly connects satisfaction with effort; this verse says the heavy-scaled person is in a pleasing life. | terra: The person with heavy scales enters عِيشَةٍ رَاضِيَةٍ, the same phrase that makes favorable reckoning visible as satisfaction.

luna: The section contrasts a pleased face with futile labor; this verse gives the opposite measure, the light scales. | terra: Light scales stage the opposite measurement: labor enters the account but lacks the weight needed for a satisfying return.

luna: The section’s contrasting efforts end in different states; this verse completes the light-scale outcome by naming its destination, Hāwiyah. | terra: The abyss is the destination produced by the light scales in 101:8, completing the failed side of the wage scene.
luna: The section links work to the final account; this neighboring question introduces the consequence of the light scales named in 101:8.

luna: The section contrasts satisfying and futile outcomes; this verse answers the preceding question with a blazing fire, completing the light-scale scene. | terra: A fiercely hot fire identifies the abyss reached by the person with light scales, completing that failed account's destination.
terra: The hoarder calculates that wealth has made him immortal; the following fire corrects a false estimate of wealth's sufficiency and lasting wage.
terra: God feeds Quraysh against hunger, a compact image of provision that truly suffices where the punishment food cannot.

luna: The section’s root gh-n-y (غ ن ي) concerns sufficiency and what does not avail; this verse says a person’s wealth and earnings will not avail him, joining failed sufficiency directly to earned means. | terra: Neither wealth nor what the condemned man earned avails him, joining failed sufficiency to acquisition in a single line.
